assemblyMapping.title: Places across an assembly change
assemblyMapping.lead: Across an assembly change, places are compared through Ensembl's own mapping of the two assemblies, and only where Ensembl publishes one.
paragraphs: Across an assembly change, places are compared through Ensembl's own mapping of the two assemblies, and only where Ensembl publishes one. Where it does (human NCBI36 to GRCh37 to GRCh38, mouse NCBIM37 to GRCm38 to GRCm39, pig Sscrofa9 to Sscrofa10.2), a gene's place on the earlier assembly is carried onto the later one and a bridge needs the two places to overlap, as on one assembly.

Compared by the names of their chromosomes alone, the mapping puts the old gene elsewhere in 7.3 % of such bridges of mouse (94 of 1,285), 1.0 % of human (44 of 4,382) and 14.8 % of pig Sscrofa9 to Sscrofa10.2 (92 of 623), counted over every gene version whose history ends, converted to release 115. Requiring an overlap also refuses the bridges that the mapping puts within a few kilobases of the gene entered without overlapping it (mouse 5, human 17 such bridges: 4 mouse and 12 human answers lost, mostly one curated gene whose model moved a little).

Where Ensembl publishes no mapping (pig Sscrofa10.2 to Sscrofa11.1, pig Sscrofa9 to Sscrofa11.1 across both changes, rhesus MMUL_1 to Mmul_8.0.1 and Mmul_8.0.1 to Mmul_10, cynomolgus Macaca_fascicularis_5.0 to 6.0), two genes are told apart across the change only by the names of their chromosomes, and how often such a bridge lands on another gene of the same chromosome is not known (pig 2,927 bridges at Sscrofa10.2 to 11.1 and 870 at Sscrofa9 to 11.1, rhesus 1,013 and 1,241, cynomolgus 917, over the gene ids gone at each change). Where a mapping is published, the names of chromosomes alone would have put 1.0 to 14.8 % of such bridges elsewhere (above); that is the only measured guide to the size.

Such a bridge can follow any identifier the old gene carried, also another gene's name: pig `convert("AKR1C3", from_release=72, to_release=115)` reads AKR1C3 as ENSSSCG00000023446 (Sscrofa10.2, last at release 89, no successor) and answers ENSSSCG00000062058, which carries AKR1C3 at 115, while `view("all")` adds ENSSSCG00000063387, reached through AKR1C1, an NCBI symbol the old gene also carried at 89: both lie on chromosome 10, which is all that the bridge can compare. In the benchmarks' comparison with other tools, 35 of the sampled wrong lines are names read at an old release and carried so across an assembly change without a published mapping (pig 24, rhesus 10, mouse 1).

mappingScore.text: Each event carries Ensembl's mapping score (0 to 1: how much of the old gene the new one keeps). A candidate's `score` is the product of the scores along its path. Ensembl writes 0 where it measured nothing between two ids; such a step has no score and a path with one ranks below every path whose scores are all measured.

items.title: Without a release, a string is what it means today
items.lead: Without a release, a string is what it means today
items.sentence: Without a release, a string is what it means today (or at the target release), by design: what it meant only at other releases is reported in `result.other_readings`, not answered.

items.title: Places across an assembly change
items.lead: Across an assembly change, places are compared through Ensembl's own mapping of the two assemblies, and only where Ensembl publishes one.
items.sentence: Across an assembly change, places are compared through Ensembl's own mapping of the two assemblies, and only where Ensembl publishes one.
items.next: Where it does (human NCBI36 to GRCh37 to GRCh38, mouse NCBIM37 to GRCm38 to GRCm39, pig Sscrofa9 to Sscrofa10.2), a gene's place on the earlier assembly is carried onto the later one and a bridge needs the two places to overlap, as on one assembly.

items.title: Copies on patches and alternative loci
items.lead: Copies on patches and alternative loci are placed by Ensembl's assembly exceptions.
items.sentence: Copies on patches and alternative loci are placed by Ensembl's assembly exceptions.
items.next: A copy's place is the region of the reference sequence that its patch or haplotype replaces at that release (Ensembl's `assembly_exception`), and a gene outside that region lies apart from it (pig and the macaques have no assembly exceptions).

items.title: Numbers that several numbering schemes share
items.lead: A string of digits is read in every database whose ids are numbers.
items.sentence: A string of digits is read in every database whose ids are numbers.
items.next: These are NCBI's gene ids, and the numeric Havana ids and RefSeq rows of early releases (reading-rules).

items.title: A branch can outrank the gene's own continuation
items.lead: A gene's own continuation does not outrank a branch that left it while it lived on.
items.sentence: A gene's own continuation does not outrank a branch that left it while it lived on.
items.next: Where Ensembl maps an id to new ids at a session while the id itself continues, the candidate on a branch can have the larger product of Ensembl's scores and become the best answer (pig `convert("ENSSSCG00000014532", from_release=56, to_release=98)` answers ENSSSCG00000042508, an offshoot, while the id's own successors rank fourth to sixth).

items.title: An id that Ensembl moves to another place
items.lead: An id that Ensembl's history carries to another place answers that id, and the result does not say that the gene moved.
items.sentence: An id that Ensembl's history carries to another place answers that id, and the result does not say that the gene moved.
items.next: Where Ensembl keeps a stable id across a version event that puts the gene on another chromosome or strand, idtrack follows the id as Ensembl does; only the explained path marks the step, and `Candidate.score`, the product of Ensembl's scores along the path, shows how weak the event is.

items.title: An id with two lives
items.lead: An id that Ensembl retired and later brought back with an old version is one node with two lives.
items.sentence: An id that Ensembl retired and later brought back with an old version is one node with two lives.
items.next: Converted into the gap between its lives, it answers by the life it starts from: human ENSG00000288686 (version 1 at 103, version 2 at 104 to 107, absent at 108 and 109, version 1 again from 110) answers XG, ENSG00000124343.14, from its first life (`convert("ENSG00000288686", from_release=107, to_release=108)`) and nothing from its second.

items.title: An id that is a transcript at some releases and a translation at others
items.lead: An Ensembl id that names a transcript at some releases and a translation at others is one node.
items.sentence: An Ensembl id that names a transcript at some releases and a translation at others is one node.
items.next: The graph keeps one node per identifier: Ensembl 107 gives a translation of IL2RB the id ENST00000515292, the id of a transcript of LINC02497 (ENSG00000251182) at releases 58 to 96, so `convert("ENST00000515292", from_release=107, to_release=107)` answers ENSG00000251182.2, not IL2RB's ENSG00000100385.15.

items.title: A symbol of the name authority can answer another gene
items.lead: At its own release, a symbol of the organism's name authority can answer another gene
items.sentence: At its own release, a symbol of the organism's name authority can answer another gene where Ensembl displays the name for both genes, or for neither, and more databases give the other gene the name: Ensembl's display name ranks first, then the support of the evidence (the authority's symbol wins against another gene's synonym only).
items.next: Of 1,500 symbols per organism, each asked at a release where the organism's symbol database names a gene with it: pig 5, rhesus 5, mouse 2, human 3 best answers include a gene the authority does not give the name (of them pig 2, rhesus 1, mouse 2 and human 2 ties with the authority's gene; were support ranked before the display name, it would be pig 10, rhesus 11, mouse 7 and human 8).

items.title: A name that another source gives another gene
items.lead: A string is read in every name source and database the graph holds at the release read, so the answer holds every gene that any of them gives it.
items.sentence: A string is read in every name source and database the graph holds at the release read, so the answer holds every gene that any of them gives it.
items.next: Ensembl's display name ranks first, then the support (concept-ranking), and the other genes are in `view("all")`: human `convert("BBS1", from_release=69, to_release=115)` answers BBS1, ENSG00000174483, and `view("all")` adds ENSG00000256349, a gene to which UniProt's gene name BBS1 is attached at 69.

items.title: A name in one letter case that another gene's link spells so
items.lead: A name in one letter case that a link of another gene spells exactly so answers that gene, not the gene the name authority displays with it in mixed case.
items.sentence: A name in one letter case that a link of another gene spells exactly so answers that gene, not the gene the name authority displays with it in mixed case.
items.next: Where, at one release, Ensembl displays a name for one mouse gene as the authority writes it and for another gene in capitals, the string in one letter case is an exact match of the links spelt so, and an exact match follows only those links (reading-matching): the authority's gene is then not among the genes reached, and the rule that ranks the authority's display name first, read without letter case, ranks only the genes reached.

items.title: Symbols typed in small letters where symbols are written in capitals
items.lead: Where an organism's symbols are written in capitals, a symbol typed with small letters can answer another gene whose synonym is spelt so.
items.sentence: Where an organism's symbols are written in capitals, a symbol typed with small letters can answer another gene whose synonym is spelt so.
items.next: The rule that reads a string against the organism's letter case first as a symbol without letter case (reading-rules) holds where symbols are written in mixed case (mouse); in pig, the macaques and human an exact synonym of another gene comes first.

items.title: Answers that only a bridge reaches
items.lead: Where Ensembl's history gives a gene no successor, an answer is the gene a bridge reaches, which no record of Ensembl states.
items.sentence: Where Ensembl's history gives a gene no successor, an answer is the gene a bridge reaches, which no record of Ensembl states.
items.next: A bridge needs an identifier that the two genes carried one after the other and places that overlap (or, across an assembly change that Ensembl publishes no mapping for, chromosomes of one name: limitation-assembly-mapping), so its gene is the plausible successor at that place, not one that Ensembl's history or the place proves.

items.title: A retired gene whose accession another gene holds today
items.lead: A gene that Ensembl retired without a successor can answer another gene than the one that holds its accessions today.
items.sentence: A gene that Ensembl retired without a successor can answer another gene than the one that holds its accessions today.
items.next: Where Ensembl retired a gene and filed its accession (an NCBI gene id, a RefSeq or UniProt accession, a miRBase accession) on another gene before, or without, giving the accession to the gene that holds it at the last release, the retired id, asked at its last release, travels by a bridge to the gene nearest in releases, not to the one the accession names now: human `ENSG00000199004` (hsa-mir-21, retired at 84 to 85) answers its host gene VMP1, which Ensembl gave NCBI's id 406991 of MIR21 at 85 to 87, while `MI0000077` and 406991 are held by ENSG00000284190, Ensembl's new miRNA gene from 88.

items.title: A split gene converted to an external database
items.lead: A gene whose history splits, converted to an external database, answers no identifier where the first-ranked of its descendants has none, although another descendant has one.
items.sentence: A gene whose history splits, converted to an external database, answers no identifier where the first-ranked of its descendants has none, although another descendant has one.
items.next: The answer is first a gene, ranked as Ensembl genes, and the identifiers are those of the genes of that best answer; where none of them has one, the result is those genes, in `view("all")` too, and the other descendants are listed as genes only.

items.title: Among the successors of a split, the best answer does not look at the old place
items.lead: Where Ensembl's history splits a gene, the best answer is ranked by Ensembl's scores and the evidence of the candidates, not by which successor lies where the old gene lay.
items.sentence: Where Ensembl's history splits a gene, the best answer is ranked by Ensembl's scores and the evidence of the candidates, not by which successor lies where the old gene lay.

items.title: RefSeq_mRNA in mouse releases 80 and 81
items.lead: In mouse releases 80 and 81, RefSeq_mRNA also holds predicted and RefSeqGene accessions.
items.sentence: In mouse releases 80 and 81, RefSeq_mRNA also holds predicted and RefSeqGene accessions.
items.next: Ensembl attaches gene-level RefSeq accessions of every kind to mouse genes at these releases under `RefSeq_dna`, which continues RefSeq_mRNA; the forms that never moved to another RefSeq database are filed under that main continuation, since RefSeq_mRNA has no identifier scheme of its own.

items.title: The support of a name counts other letter cases
items.lead: The support of a name counts a database that writes it in another letter case.
items.sentence: The support of a name counts a database that writes it in another letter case.
items.next: Typed in mixed case, a mouse symbol is the display name only as its database spelt it, but the number of databases that attach it to a gene counts UniProt's gene name in capitals too.

items.title: Single-cell suffixes after a name that is no authority's symbol
items.lead: A suffix of single-cell tools after a name that is no symbol of the name authority at the release asked about can be read into another gene's synonym.
items.sentence: A suffix of single-cell tools after a name that is no symbol of the name authority at the release asked about can be read into another gene's synonym.
items.next: The rule that keeps `SRF.1` from SPATA6's synonym `SRF-1` (reading-rules) needs the string before the suffix to be a symbol that a name authority gives at the release asked about (without a release, the target release), also where the synonym is read at another release.

items.title: The GRCh37 gene ids of LRG records list their answer among the copies
items.lead: An LRG record's gene id of the GRCh37 releases answers the gene the record describes, but its result lists that gene among the copies set apart, and not the record.
items.sentence: An LRG record's gene id of the GRCh37 releases answers the gene the record describes, but its result lists that gene among the copies set apart, and not the record.

items.title: Low-9 quotation marks
items.lead: Low-9 quotation marks are not read as quotes.
items.sentence: Low-9 quotation marks are not read as quotes.
items.next: The quotation marks removed around an identifier are Unicode's initial and final quotes and the ASCII ones (reading-cleaning); the low-9 marks that open a quotation in German and other languages belong to Unicode's category of opening punctuation together with the brackets, and no property of Unicode tells the two apart, so `„TP53“` and `‚TP53‘` are not found (never another gene).

items.title: Databases the graph does not hold
items.lead: Identifiers of databases that the graph does not hold answer nothing.
items.sentence: Identifiers of databases that the graph does not hold answer nothing.
items.next: A graph holds the databases that its externals configuration selects, and the shipped configurations do not select RNAcentral, the name authorities' own ids (HGNC, MGI and VGNC ids), UniProt's secondary accessions and entry names (but the entry names that early releases display as genes' names) or UniProt's isoforms.

items.title: MGI's symbols of mouse releases 48 to 54 that are Havana ids
items.lead: At mouse releases 48 to 54, a gene whose MGI symbol was its Havana id has no MGI symbol in a conversion.
items.sentence: At mouse releases 48 to 54, a gene whose MGI symbol was its Havana id has no MGI symbol in a conversion.
items.next: MGI gave genes without a symbol of their own their Havana gene id as their symbol, and Ensembl's records of those releases file it as the gene's `MGI Symbol` label.

items.title: miRBase's names on miRNA genes only
items.lead: The graph holds miRBase's names and accessions on genes of a miRNA biotype only, and leaves out an entry that Ensembl gives to genes at two loci.
items.sentence: The graph holds miRBase's names and accessions on genes of a miRNA biotype only, and leaves out an entry that Ensembl gives to genes at two loci.
items.next: Such a name therefore answers the miRNA gene, or nothing, where Ensembl's records give it to other genes too (changes, 0.1.0).

items.title: Synonyms that are fragments of UniProt's evidence text
items.lead: A few synonyms are fragments of UniProt's evidence text.
items.sentence: A few synonyms are fragments of UniProt's evidence text.
items.next: The graph drops a synonym that carries the evidence UniProt writes in a gene name, but where Ensembl's rows split such a text, the piece without its opening brace stays a synonym of the gene: human 45 synonyms, mouse 20, pig and the macaques none (`api.genes_named("GNECO:0000312|HGNC:HGNC:11125}")` gives UniProt's synonym of SUMO2, ENSG00000188612, at release 79).

items.title: Ensembl's cross references against the databases' own files
items.lead: An identifier of another database answers the gene Ensembl's cross-references give it, also where the database's own file says otherwise.
items.sentence: An identifier of another database answers the gene Ensembl's cross-references give it, also where the database's own file says otherwise.
items.next: Ensembl's tables are the record idtrack reads; where NCBI, RefSeq or UniProt give an identifier another gene, or none, in their own files, the answer is still Ensembl's gene.

items.meaning: Identifiers: Ensembl gene, transcript and translation ids with their versions, and the ids and names of the external databases the graph holds (HGNC and NCBI symbols, RefSeq and UniProt accessions, NCBI gene ids, ...: databases).

Ensembl's id history (its `mapping_session` and `stable_id_event` tables): an id that continues with a new version, is replaced, split or merged between two releases, with Ensembl's mapping score of the event.
At a release, an Ensembl gene (or one of its transcripts or translations) carries an id of an external database. Every such edge holds for the releases at which Ensembl's tables give it.
External ids that the build left out because they are Ensembl ids (an Ensembl node or a gene's base id).
Where a gene lies: on which assembly, sequence region, bases and strand, at which releases.
A gene's places on the reference sequence carried onto later assemblies by Ensembl's mapping.
Ensembl's assembly exceptions of the graph's releases: which reference region each patch or haplotype is.
